title: Adi Dassler, a Divided Factory and a Handwritten 'i' in 1949
dek: In 1948 the Dassler brothers split their shoe firm in two; a year later Adi registered adidas with 47 staff, and the brothers never spoke again.

story.event: Splitting the family shoe firm with his brother Rudolf and registering adidas
story.summary: In 1948 Adi and Rudolf Dassler ended the sports-shoe firm they had run together in Herzogenaurach after years of quarrels; Rudolf took one factory and founded what became Puma, while Adi kept the other and most of the staff. On 18 August 1949 Adi registered his company, adding a handwritten 'i' to the planned name addas, and started with 47 employees and a three-strap football boot whose straps became the three stripes. The brothers never spoke again.
paragraphs: On 3 February 1947, a Bavarian state office told Adi Dassler in Herzogenaurach that he could run his own shoe factory again. A denazification tribunal had first barred him from owning a business; he and his brother Rudolf had both joined the Nazi party in 1933. Reclassified as a "follower", he was back in charge of a firm that had kept going by making sports shoes from war leftovers: tent canvas, rubber rafts, the rubberised fabric of aircraft fuel tanks.

He also had a brother he could no longer work with. In 1943, after Rudolf was drafted, he had asked to be told of every business decision and wanted his wife to act for him; Adi refused, and their letters turned hostile. After the war Rudolf was held by the Americans for about a year, and he came to believe Adi had arranged it, which Adi denied. The two families shared a villa, and the wives did not get along.

In 1948 the brothers broke up the firm they had run together for more than twenty years. Rudolf took the second factory, on Würzburger Strasse, and started the company that became Puma. Adi kept the works by the railway station, and most of the staff, many of them people who developed and made the shoes, chose to stay with him. On 18 August 1949, aged 48, he entered his new company in the commercial register. He had meant to call it addas, but a children's shoe maker already used the name, so he added an "i" by hand on the form. He began with 47 employees. The year before, he had designed a football boot with three parallel straps to hold the foot steady; the straps became the company's mark.

The business grew. In 1954 West Germany won the World Cup final in Bern wearing his lightweight boots with screw-in studs, and the three stripes became known far beyond Bavaria. The breach did not heal. In Herzogenaurach, split by the river Aurach between the two factories, families, bakeries and pubs took sides. The brothers never spoke to each other again, and they were buried at opposite ends of the town cemetery. In 2009, six decades on, employees of the two companies played a friendly football match on mixed teams.

quote.text: Set out, therefore, after a violent quarrel; be at peace with him that is hostile unto [thee] his opponent. It is such souls that make love to grow.
quote.work: The Instruction of Ptahhotep (and of Ke'gemni)
quote.source_title: The Instruction of Ptah-Hotep and the Instruction of Ke'Gemni, tr. Battiscombe G. Gunn, Project Gutenberg eBook #30508
quote.connection: Ptahhotep puts two steps side by side: leave after the quarrel, and then make peace with the one who is hostile. Adi Dassler took the first and built a company on it. The second never came, and a whole town lived in the gap for decades.

reflection: Some partings at work are necessary. The Dassler brothers wanted different things from the same firm, and dividing it let each build what he believed in. What the division did not do was settle the grievance underneath. Each man carried it for the rest of his life, and so did the workers, shopkeepers and families around them.

Over the years you will part ways with people: a colleague, a collaborator, perhaps someone you once built with. Dividing the work is usually the easier half. The harder half is whether you leave room for an ordinary word between you afterwards, even if you never work together again.
invitation: Think of one working relationship that ended badly or has simply gone quiet. You do not have to mend it today. Write one sentence you could honestly say to that person if you met, and keep it somewhere you will find it.

cross_checks.claim: The brothers split the firm in 1948, Rudolf founding what became Puma and Adi keeping the other factory and most of the staff.
Adi registered the company on 18 August 1949 and began with 47 employees.
The planned name addas was changed by adding an 'i' because a children's shoe maker already used it.
Rudolf was held by the Americans for about a year and believed his brother was behind it.
The brothers never reconciled and were buried at opposite ends of the town cemetery.

research_notes: Staff split: the Dassler foundation says about two-thirds of the workforce stayed with Adi; the 2019 dpa report in Abendzeitung says 47 stayed with Adi and 13 chose Rudolf (about four-fifths); adidas gives 47 employees at the 1949 start without saying how many went to Rudolf. The story says 'most of the staff' and uses 47 only as Adi's starting headcount, which adidas and dpa agree on. Age: adidas's history page says Adi started 'at the age of 49', but his birth date, given by both adidas and the foundation as 3 November 1900, makes him 48 on 18 August 1949, so the story says 48. Founding of the joint firm: Business Insider and others give 1919; adidas and dpa give the registration of the Gebrüder Dassler Schuhfabrik as 1924, so the story says only 'more than twenty years'. Cause of the split: accounts differ and Business Insider notes historians still disagree; the story gives the documented strands (the 1943 letters, from the foundation; Rudolf's belief that Adi caused his internment, which the foundation says Adi denied and Smit describes as Rudolf's conviction; the wives' friction, from Fortune and Smit) and does not adjudicate. The well-known bomb-shelter anecdote in Fortune is omitted because it is told only as legend. The foundation is run by Adi's family and is sympathetic to him; its account of his Nazi-era conduct is not relied on beyond the documented tribunal classifications and the 3 February 1947 letter it reproduces. Three stripes: the foundation says the three-strap boot was developed the year before the 1949 registration; adidas says a shoe with the three stripes was registered in 1949; the story uses both. The quote is Gunn's maxim 26; the bracketed '[thee]' is the translator's own insertion and is kept as printed.
